topics: 🐄 New Mishna: The Substitute of a Firstborn or Tithe — grazed, blemished, then eaten
🩹 May One Blemish the Substitute of a Firstborn or Tithe?
🌍 Ben Antigonus's Rejected Firstborns — a contradiction resolved
📜 Three Elders, Three Rulings — bringing bikkurim-like offerings from outside Eretz Yisrael
☠️ New Mishna: Recapping the Sin Offerings Left to Die

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing Chapter Three, Opening Chapter Four
overview.subtitle: Temurah 21a–21b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna describes the substitute of a firstborn or animal tithe offering: unlike other substitutes, it is never sacrificed on the altar, but grazes until blemished and is then eaten (by priests for a firstborn, by owners for a tithe) — with several practical differences from ordinary consecrated animals, including that unblemished ones may even be brought from outside Eretz Yisrael. The Gemara asks whether inflicting a blemish on such a substitute carries liability, resolving it by analogy to the 'ninth' animal miscounted during tithing. A striking contradiction — the mishna permits unblemished firstborns from outside the land, yet a story shows ben Antigonus's were rejected — is resolved by attributing each ruling to a different tanna among three elders, whose logic for various 'must be eaten in the Temple's presence' halakhot (second tithe, firstborn, first fruits) is explored at length. The daf ends Chapter Three and opens Chapter Four with a mishna recapping which sin offerings are left to die.

slides.title: 🐄 New Mishna: The Firstborn/Tithe Substitute Is Different
slides.subtitle: Four ways it departs from every other kind of substitute
rows: Butchers' market (איטליז), weighed by the litra
Only from the home — never in the market, never by weight
Yes — sold, proceeds sacred, animal non-sacred
No redemption at all — it stays consecrated until eaten in its blemished state
Only if it arrives unblemished; if blemished, eaten locally by owner/priest
Firstborn's substitute: the priests. Tithe's substitute: the owners

callout.label: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning:
callout.text: Firstborn and tithe animals have 'sustenance in their own place' — they can be eaten once blemished without needing to reach the Temple — unlike ordinary consecrated animals, which must be redeemed for a proper offering.

slides.title: 🩹 Is One Liable for Blemishing This Substitute?
slides.subtitle: A dilemma resolved by analogy to the mistakenly-counted 'ninth' tithe animal

nodes.content: ❓ Since the substitute of a firstborn/tithe is never sacrificed on the altar, does the Torah's prohibition against blemishing a sacrificial animal even apply to it?
🔀 Compare: the 'ninth' animal mistakenly counted as the tenth during tithing — also consecrated (can't be worked or sheared) but also never reaches the altar
📖 For the ninth: the verse 'the TENTH shall be holy' excludes it — so blemishing it carries NO liability
✅ Same logic applies here: 'THEY (the firstborn/tithe) are holy' (Num. 18:17) — THEY are sacrificed, not their substitute — so blemishing the substitute carries no liability either

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Wherever a verse explicitly limits altar-sacrifice to the 'original' item and excludes a derivative, that same exclusion extends to the blemishing prohibition too.

slides.title: 🌍 Why Were Ben Antigonus's Firstborns Rejected?
slides.subtitle: A direct contradiction with the mishna's own ruling, resolved by dividing the halakha between two tanna'im

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: Firstborn and tithe offerings should not be brought from outside Eretz Yisrael ab initio, but if unblemished ones DID arrive, they ARE sacrificed.

lines.speaker: Historical account
lines.text: But ben Antigonus actually brought firstborns up from Babylonia — and the Temple did NOT accept them!

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda resolves
lines.text: No contradiction: the mishna follows Rabbi Yishmael (accepts them after the fact), while ben Antigonus's rejection follows Rabbi Akiva (never accepts them, even unblemished).

lines.speaker: Rabbi Akiva's proof
lines.text: 'You shall eat... the tithe of your grain... and the firstborn of your herd' (Deut. 14:23) — only from a place you bring UP grain tithe (i.e., Eretz Yisrael) may you bring a firstborn at all.

callout.label: Deeper stakes:
callout.text: This dispute belongs to a set of three teachings by three elders (Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva, ben Azzai), each addressing how far consecrated status extends geographically.

slides.title: 📜 Three Elders' Methods: Analogy vs. Juxtaposition
slides.subtitle: Each elder tries — and refines — an inference before landing on the right verse

boxes.title: Rejected: Simple Analogy (Kal Vachomer-style)
items: 'Second tithe requires bringing to a place, like a firstborn — so it too can't be eaten today'
Refuted: a firstborn uniquely requires blood/portions on the altar; second tithe has no such requirement
The two cases aren't comparable enough to infer directly

boxes.title: Accepted: Direct Verse Juxtaposition
items: Deuteronomy 14:23 lists tithe of grain AND firstborn in one verse
This textual juxtaposition (הֶקֵּשׁ) directly links their halakhot, bypassing the need for logical analogy
Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule: sacrificial law generally can't be derived from a law that was ITSELF derived — but second tithe is non-sacred, so this restriction doesn't block the inference

callout.label: Ben Azzai's parallel move:
callout.text: He similarly first tries (and rejects) a simple analogy to prove second tithe must be eaten specifically within Jerusalem's walls, before landing on the same verse's juxtaposition to reach that conclusion.

slides.title: ☠️ New Mishna: Recapping the Sin Offerings Left to Die
slides.subtitle: Chapter Four opens by restating and refining the earlier list
rows: Year passed, OR lost-and-found-blemished AFTER owner's atonement
Left to die — and critically, does NOT generate a substitute at all

callout.label: New emphasis:
callout.text: This mishna sharpens a point implicit earlier: an animal already destined to die cannot generate a valid temurah — reinforcing that only animals with a live path to the altar can be substituted for.

summary.principle: The substitute of a firstborn or tithe is uniquely never sacrificed, sold only from home, and exempt from blemishing liability just like the original — while unblemished firstborns from outside Eretz Yisrael divide Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, whose competing methods (juxtaposition vs. simple analogy) also settle several related 'must eat in the Temple's presence' halakhot.

flowSteps.content: 🐄 Firstborn/tithe substitute: never sacrificed, sold only from home, no redemption
🩹 Blemishing it carries no liability — 'they are holy,' not their substitute

columns.content: 🌍 R' Yishmael: unblemished firstborns from outside the land ARE accepted
🌍 R' Akiva: they are NEVER accepted (ben Antigonus's case)

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: verse juxtaposition (hekesh), not simple analogy, is what properly transfers a halakha between different sacred categories

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens to the substitute of a firstborn or tithe offering once it develops a blemish?
o: It is sold in the butchers' market like other consecrated animals
It is redeemed and becomes fully non-sacred
It is eaten in its blemished state — by priests (firstborn) or owners (tithe) — never sold at the market or redeemed
It is always left to die
quiz.e: Unlike ordinary substitutes, a firstborn's or tithe's substitute is never redeemed or sold by weight in the market; once blemished it is simply eaten by the appropriate party (priest or owner) directly.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the question of whether one is liable for inflicting a blemish on the substitute of a firstborn or tithe?
o: By citing an explicit verse specifically about blemishing
By analogy to the 'ninth' tithe animal, excluded from altar-sacrifice by 'the TENTH shall be holy' — similarly, 'THEY are holy' (Num. 18:17) excludes the substitute, so no liability applies
By saying blemishing is always forbidden regardless
By concluding the question remains permanently unresolved
quiz.e: The Gemara draws a parallel to the excluded 'ninth' animal from tithing, concluding that just as that exclusion removes blemishing liability, the verse 'they are holy' (excluding the substitute from the altar) removes it here too.

quiz.q: How does Rav Ḥisda resolve the contradiction between the mishna (accepting unblemished firstborns from outside Eretz Yisrael) and the story of ben Antigonus (whose firstborns were rejected)?
o: He says the story of ben Antigonus never happened
He attributes the mishna to Rabbi Yishmael and the rejection to Rabbi Akiva's stricter view
He says both sources agree completely
He claims firstborns were never brought from outside the land
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda resolves the contradiction by assigning each ruling to a different tanna: the mishna's lenient acceptance follows Rabbi Yishmael, while ben Antigonus's rejection follows Rabbi Akiva's stricter position.

quiz.q: What method does the Gemara ultimately accept for deriving that second tithe must be eaten only in Jerusalem's presence, after a simple analogy is refuted?
o: Pure logical inference with no verse needed
A direct verse juxtaposition (hekesh) in Deuteronomy 14:23 linking grain tithe and firstborn in one verse
A tradition from Sinai with no textual source
The question is left completely unresolved
quiz.e: After the simple analogy to a firstborn is refuted (firstborns uniquely require altar placement), the Gemara accepts the direct textual juxtaposition in Deuteronomy 14:23, which links the two halakhot without needing independent logical proof.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna opening Chapter Four, what is emphasized about a sin offering that was lost and found blemished AFTER the owner already achieved atonement?
o: It may still be sacrificed on the altar
It is left to die and does NOT generate a substitute
It becomes a burnt offering automatically
It is given to the poor
quiz.e: The mishna stresses that this sin offering, like the others in its list, is left to die and critically does not generate a valid temurah — reinforcing that an animal with no path to the altar cannot be substituted for.
